utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-01-42-T, the Prosecutor versus Pavle Strugar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, everybody. If I could remind you, Mr. Stringer, that the affirmation you took is still applicable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Rodic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Stringer. I will continue cross-examination today. It will be significantly shorter than yesterday, so let us begin. Item 11 of your diary, which lists the team which took part in negotiations. So this is the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik, Zeljko Sikic, Hrvoje Makan, and Misa, and another name. After Misa, in parenthesis it states "interpreter." This is what your diary shows as an entry of that event; however, in the statement you gave to investigators, next to Misa it says Mihocevic, the last name and then it says producer of the festival and interpreter for the monitoring mission. Could you please tell me who supplied you with the last name of this interpreter and the function of this person.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpreter's name was given to me by his card, as producer of the Dubrovnik Festival.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understood that. However, you never listed this person's last name in your diary, nor did you list this person's role, the one mentioned in the statement. However, the statement was given to investigators based on your memory and using the notes you made in your diary. So what I would like to know is whether somebody supplied you with the last name of this person, because the statement was given ten years after the events.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. At the time I wrote in the diary Misa, because that was how we knew him. But he then later gave us his card and I had a copy -- the actual -- one of his cards which had his name on it, so it was helpful to put the surname as well as the first name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The general is not receiving interpretation, so we need to see what is the matter. Could the usher please put before the witness Exhibit P4, which is a handwritten diary which the witness gave to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at paragraph 44 of your diary. Could you please read it out loud to us.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Prior to the 1500 hours meeting, the team visited a children's hospital at Cavtat opposite the JNA front line, run by a Sarajevo charity. The team was also shown holes in windows and walls caused by small arms fire were told that one round had penetrated a ward at 0415 that morning." 3

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does your diary indicate that you had been shown holes in windows and walls caused by fire from infantry weapons?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, that is so, but I can't confirm that at this stage, at this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told that a bullet entered a hospital ward at 4.15 that morning?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what my statement says in the diary, and I have no reason to doubt the veracity of my annotation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that means that we can conclude that this was not a shell that pierced the wall, because there is an obvious difference between a shell piercing the wall and a wall being damaged by artillery round, or a window being pierced by an artillery round. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm or -- I can't confirm whether it was an artillery round or a small arms fire at this time because I do not recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please also give to the witness the typed-up report dated 16th October, which was given to all the parties yesterday and marked with an ID number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I just say, Mr. Rodic -- could I just say that I don't believe any statement has been marked at this point. It was given to us, and we were waiting to see what, if any, use was made of it, to see whether or not it might be admitted. Now, did you have some other point, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That was my question. I wasn't aware of any document being marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to do that at the end of the hearing today. Nevertheless, this document dated October 16th, in our view, should be given an ID number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I'm interested in item 9. Could you please read it out.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We immediately drove to our fishing boat to have a message relayed over the coastal radio system to General Strugar at Kumbor, Bay of Kotor, expressing our concern at this turn of events and asking him immediately to have the ultimatum withdrawn and announced to the villagers by loudspeaker. He was also asked to withdraw his patrols which were causing extreme alarm to the local population."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you read out everything that is stated in that item? Is Kumbor perhaps mentioned somewhere in the text?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say Kumbor. "We immediately drove to our fishing boat to have a message relayed over the coastal radio system to General Strugar at Kumbor (Bay of Kotor)."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your communication normally go through the radio with the coast guard in Kumbor, and was it used frequently -- were messages relayed in this manner frequently?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall precisely how many messages were relayed by that means. But on that occasion, certainly, that was the only means of transmitting a message.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Related to this, I would like to ask you whether you always -- when you sent messages to the JNA, did you always send them to Kumbor first, as the centre receiving such messages?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know any other place where you might have sent messages, or did perhaps somebody else indicate another place where you could send messages?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't confirm that at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please put before the witness his statement given to the Prosecutors and discussed yesterday, the one in English which also hasn't been given a number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the witness please go to page 14 of the English version. This is the part where you explain item 7(A). I'm interested in this particular sentence, the second one. Where it states: "However, as time went on, it became clear that the JNA negotiating team, except for Jokic, always deferred to the operational commander." Did you state this?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask you to take a look at the bottom of the page, last paragraph. The following sentence -- I will read it out: "Jokic was in charge of the first real negotiations. He was a vice-admiral, and I think that as such, as a commander of the naval centre, Jokic also took over command or responsibility for all weapons and all units in this campaign. It was completely clear to me that he can adopt decisions or influence the decision-making and pass orders concerning land forces." I would like to know whether you concluded this as a result of your contacts with Jokic or naval officers during your stay in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the assumption that we made after our discussions with Admiral Jokic and certainly up to the time that Captain Zec handed us -- up until the time certainly when we were handed a letter from General Ruzinovski advising us of his change of command. It's thereafter, as my notes do indicate, the liaison officer always had to go back to General Strugar for advice as to the questions we asked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you then explain to us why did you state something like this to investigators? Because this is a clarification that you are giving here in this statement concerning Admiral Jokic and his role in negotiations.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't occur to me at the time, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of making the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is this something that investigators put into the statement, or is this something that you have stated?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my statement, but it didn't occur to me. I perhaps should have thought further and made a further clarification as to the responsibilities of the various military officers. But it was Jokic with whom the ball lay, if I may put it that way, certainly up to the time of the change of command of the generals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree with that, and this is in accord with this quotation that I have just read out. I will now turn to another question. Further in this statement please take a look at the clarification you gave concerning item 21. First paragraph, last sentence in the first paragraph: "This left us with no doubt that the naval officers were very much part and parcel of this operation and had significant influence or command over its execution."

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the following paragraph you say -- I apologise, not the following paragraph, but the penultimate paragraph concerning item 21 in your statement. You say that: "A list of conditions that was handed to the Croats was signed on behalf of Jokic or by Jokic." This is another example of the command responsibility of Admiral Miodrag Jokic. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the following page when you give clarification, as per item 26, the second paragraph, you say: "I personally informed the JNA leadership, including Jokic, that in the hotels around Cavtat and in Cavtat there were thousands of refugees." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please take a look at the clarification given for item 76, where the message or the letter of General Strugar is mentioned. So this is your clarification for item 76. I will quote. You turned over to investigators a copy of the letter of General Strugar and then you go on to explain: "The letter spoke of provocation by the Croats and I have little doubt that this was indeed a provocation." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the letter spoke of provocation by the Croats and I have little doubt that this may, in fact, have happened, because there were renegade Croats we believe, as I say in my statement here, who may have tried to undermine any bona fide effort by all sides to restore peace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Also in this part where you give explanation for item 76, in the following paragraph you say: "As to the reference to a canon at the Hotel Croatia, I think that this hotel was in Cavtat, but I cannot comment on the veracity of this allegation." Is this true?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The following page, when you discuss the telephone message by Lieutenant Colonel General Strugar -- just a minute, please, I need to find the sentence.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... goes to page 16, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So below the place where it's indicated Lieutenant Colonel General Pavle Strugar, so right in that area. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just trying to look at the piece of document that you have. Can you repeat, I'm sorry, where you're asking me to look. Page 16?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is indicated in bold letters: "Message by telephone from Colonel General Strugar 0030 16/" and so on.

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at the end of the text concerning that statement, again in bold letters, you have Lieutenant General Pavle Strugar. And right below that, it's on page 17, "It is possible that this message had come in through Dubrovnik Crisis Staff, because they had both radio and telephone connection with the JNA in Kumbor. And this is the connection that we used to establish contact with the JNA." Is this true?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it says there, yes. I can't recall, I'm afraid, at this point in time precisely what the communication link was. But at the time that I wrote this, I believe that to be correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then at the end, in the report of the parliamentary assembly of the Council of Europe, in September of 1993, on page 24, under the subheadline "Cultural Vandalism in the Old Town," it is stated that: "The monuments in the Old Town concerning the Second World War had been destroyed by explosives, explosive material." So this happened in the Old Town. Do you know anything about this, did you learn anything of this during your stay on the mission in Dubrovnik? Had you heard anything of this or did you learn anything about this?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, I would like to repeat what you have said here before this Court, namely that you never met General Strugar, that you never spoke to him directly, that your contacts were only with naval officers Jokic, Zec, Sofronije Jeremic, interpreter Uljarevic. Then you also said that everything that Croatia and the JNA submitted to you was related to you by other persons, namely interpreters. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object to that question, Your Honour; that's a speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Rodic, you might rephrase it to say: Did you also say those things?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I agree, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let me repeat, Mr. Stringer: Have you said -- is it true that you never met General Strugar personally, that you never spoke to him directly, that you only contacted naval officers Admiral Jokic, Captain Zec, and Sofronije Jeremic, Colonel Svicevic, interpreter Uljarevic, and that all messages, both from the Croatian Crisis Staff and from the JNA were conveyed to you through interpreters?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you have to add General Ruzinovski to that list of officers with whom we spoke, because he conducted the initial meeting, of course. And I believe there was one other army officer that we met there. I think that is in my notes. But otherwise, yes, the -- I had not -- I never met General Strugar personally, nor did we speak to him. We merely tried to make contact but were unable to do so. The messages were conveyed. I can't confirm exactly who -- the mode of communication. That came through our interpreter, Misa. Some must have come through the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the messages that were described as messages from General Strugar were indeed messages that he personally had sent?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my belief, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another brief question: When you returned from your mission in Dubrovnik, you said that in London, at the Ministry for Defence, you took over as the director for security of physical persons, buildings, and facilities. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, basically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was somebody else performing those duties before you who namely served as the director for security?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I succeeded a person who had been director of security before me, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you -- I assume this is correct, and you can correct me if I'm wrong, did you go through the formal procedure of taking over your new responsibilities? And if so, can you tell us, how long did this period last for, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My responsibilities after I left Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I mean when you took over in your new capacity as director for security department and the Ministry of Defence. So when you took over this job from your predecessor, how long did this transition process last for, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall, maybe a day. But it's one of these things that is continuing, because I believe my successor, in fact, took up a job above me. I can't recall precisely how long the handover took.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, I assume that it was longer than one day. It took you longer than one day to understand and comprehend all these new responsibilities that you assumed?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really, because I had been a deputy director before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have concluded by cross-examination. Thank you, Mr. Stringer. Could Mr. Stringer's statement please be given an exhibit number, tendered into evidence, including the statement dating October 16th. Could that be given an ID number, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you have any submission in respect of the two statements, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We have no objection to Mr. Stringer's statement being given a number and tendered into evidence. And we would have no objection if they would like the second statement tendered into evidence, too, his statement indicated "Note an incident at Dubrovnik."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think both of those that Mr. Rodic indicated should be --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Both the statement given to the investigators on the 26th and 27th March of 1992, and the other document dated, I think, Note, and given on the 16th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The two documents will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the statement of Mr. Stringer dated 27th March, 2002, would be given Exhibit Number D1; and the note made by Mr. Stringer, D2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Weiner, do you re-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, please. Re-examined by Mr. Weiner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Mr. Stringer. After General Strugar assumed command, did you have any contact with Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After General Strugar assumed command, who made the decisions in relation to your requests?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ECMM's position or view of the chain of command with regard to General Strugar and Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that whilst Admiral Jokic did have command responsibilities, the overall commander was, in fact, the general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which general?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Strugar at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when General Ruzinovski was the commander of the 2nd Operational Group, what was the ECMM's team view of General Jokic's position in relation to General Ruzinovski?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that at one point General Ruzinovski ordered Admiral Jokic to take part in the negotiations. Were you surprised at that?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not particularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in so many of these situations there tends to be joint command, inter-service command, and you would not expect perhaps the supreme commander to be concerned with the minutiae of negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there was some discussion in relation to the interpreter that you were using. At your meetings, did the JNA also have an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any point during any of those negotiations, did the JNA Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. interpreter complain that something was not being properly translated?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there ever a complaint from anyone in the JNA that your interpreter was not properly translating matters?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that on or about the 15th or on the 15th of October, you sent a message to General Strugar concerning the incident that you had seen, the shooting and the loudspeaker. Was General Strugar present when you sent that message through the coastguard at the coastal radio system?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were told that he was not available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they say what they were going to do with your message?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were going to pass the message to his headquarters for immediate attention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And just two matters in relation to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit D1, his statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at page 15, at the bottom of page 15 of that document. And it says: "A hand report" -- above that, I'm sorry. In relation to -- that's right. The last line: "I hand a report that further covers events on the 16th of October and mark it ..." The incident where you had the meeting and then the shooting that occurred, did that occur on the 16th, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think that was the 15th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then if you go to the next page, sir, page 17, the first line. It says at the top: "On the 17th, I received a message from General Strugar." And then if you go down to the middle of the page, it has the message and it's dated on the 16th. What was the date of that message?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 16th. The confusion arose, I think, because it was about midnight and it was the -- in between the two dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the last thing I want to discuss with you is on page 3. On page 3, paragraph -- the third full paragraph. The second sentence: "The Croats did possess defensive weapons, although they were mainly small arms, with some smaller artillery or anti-tank weapons." Did you ever see any smaller artillery or anti-tank weapons within the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see those weapons, the artillery or anti-tank weapons?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't personally see these weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your information, what does that refer to then?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information, I believe, refers to advice that we were given, either by the JNA or by the Croats themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now it says: "The JNA" -- if we go down two more sentences. "The JNA were without doubt in the driving seat and totally in control of areas they occupied. They could dictate the pace or intensity of any battle as they pleased and any purported retaliation to cease-fire breaches seemed to be more punitive than out of military necessity." Could you tell me first what you meant by your statement: "The JNA seemed without a doubt to be in the driving seat"?

utterances.speaker: ADRIEN STRINGER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they had the dominating positions around Dubrovnik, around the airport, and there was no way that Croatians could leave that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I believe we have -- I'm sorry, Mr. Weiner, I assumed that you were saying that was the end of your --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. I've completed re-direct examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stringer, you have come, I believe, to the end of your evidence. May I thank you for your attendance here and the assistance that you've given to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're now free to leave if you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, the question of the next witness and one of time. How practical is it, do you think, to commence the witness with the hope of finishing the evidence today?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I think Mr. Kaufman, who is handling that witness, would be better to address that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I anticipate that the examination-in-chief should be somewhere in the region of half an hour to an hour. I have spoken to my learned friend Mr. Petrovic, and he anticipates that the cross-examination - I'm sure he'll correct me if I misrepresent what he told me - will be considerably shorter than the cross-examination of Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned colleague is quite right. It will, of course, be shorter than Mr. Stringer's interrogation, but whether we will finish by 6.00, it's difficult to say. I cannot specify the exact time. So it is up to you, Your Honours, to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kaufman, I fear that it's going to be necessary for the witness to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness is prepared for that eventuality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If that is the case, is there a great deal to be gained by proceeding with part of the evidence this afternoon or not? How do you see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Well, I leave that matter -- if I may just consult with Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're quite happy to leave the matter to the discretion of the Court. We're quite happy to start examination-in-chief today. But if the Court feels it would rather that the cross-examination and examination-in-chief take place on one day, then we would leave that matter to the Court's discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is of the view, Mr. Kaufman, that we would take the evidence in-chief of the witness now, but would then adjourn, with cross-examination on the 12th of January. If you think that will fit in with your situation, we could proceed to call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, bearing in mind, therefore, that the proceedings today will be considerably shortened, I would beg Your Honour's request for maybe a five-minute interval so that we can set up a stand in court, because I intend on presenting some maps during the evidence of the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What we might do, then, is to have a break perhaps a little longer than five minutes to ensure that Mr. Strugar can relax for a little while, and we will resume at a little after 20 past. --- Break taken at 3.11 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness is sworn in, I have some exhibits which I would like to present to the Court by virtue of agreement between myself and Mr. Petrovic. There's no need to introduce them through this witness, they can be submitted at this stage. We're talking about maps, maps of the Dubrovnik region and the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you then, Mr. Kaufman. If that's by agreement between counsel, then you can proceed to do that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The first map is a map of -- entitled "The Times Map of the Western Balkans." It depicts the former Yugoslavia -- or at least, Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Dubrovnik area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be Exhibit P9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: The second map I would wish to introduce is a map entitled "Croatia City Graphic." It is a cartographer's map and I would request that this map be displayed on the stand once it has been given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Dubrovnik city -- what was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sorry, it's "Croatia City Graphic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. "Croatia City Graphic." That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be marked, Your Honour, as P10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I wonder if one of those maps may be put on the stand. Your Honours, the third map is entitled "Dubrovnik City Map."

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be P11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: The fourth and penultimate map is entitled "Dubrovnik." It portrays the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that would be marked P12, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: The fifth and final map, I will call it "Cultural Monuments Map" because it is also entitled "Dubrovnik Old Town" and we already have that title. So if we could call this map "Cultural Monuments and Old Town Map."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be P12 -- P13, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: P13, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I thank Your Honours for their indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If the witness would now take the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Kaufman. Examined by Mr. Kaufman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you state your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: My name is John Bartlett Allcock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is Allcock with two Ls, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Allcock with two Ls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your title?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: At the moment, I have an honourary title; Honourary Reader in the Sociology of South-Eastern Europe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will refer to you as Dr. Allcock.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your age, please, sir?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And present address.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: My present address is -- You mean my domestic address rather than university address. Is Broadfolds House, "Broadfolds" is one word and spelled as it would be expected to. Chrisharben Park in the area of Clayton, which is part of Bradford, and the postal code is BD14 6AE.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Allcock, before we formally tender your expert report, which has already been submitted to the Trial Chamber, I would like to ask you a few questions about your curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you are now retired but what was your last position that you held?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: The last position I held until the end of July two years ago was as reader in sociology at the University of Bradford.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now that you have retired, what are your current academic concerns?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I continue to spend a certain amount of my time in sociological writing and covering a variety topics. The principal thing which concerns me at the moment is a study of the political response to the existence of this Tribunal within the countries of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Allcock, I don't wish to go into the list of all your publications, which are appended to your expert report, but if I may just draw your attention to perhaps your last major published work. Can you tell the Court what that was.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: That was the book entitled "Explaining Yugoslavia," published jointly by Christopher Hurst in London and the Columbia University Press. And this was a large-scale study from the point of view of historical sociology of the nature of the Yugoslav Federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that you are also the chief editor of a work entitled "An Encyclopedia, the Balkan Conflict."

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: That's not quite the title, but I get the idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct me and perhaps tell the Court the correct title, and let us know a bit about that publication.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I shall have to look up the correct title myself now that you've given me the wrong one. The correct title is "Conflict in the Former Yugoslavia, an Encyclopedia." And this appeared as one of a series of major conflict problems throughout the world, published by ABC Clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you received reviews of your work, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes, quite a few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have there been any reviews from the former republics?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes; in fact only this week I came across one published in a well-respected Belgrade journal Tokovi Istorije by Professor Mile Bjelajac, who is a professor at the Institute for Modern History in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the expert report which will be tendered to the Trial Chamber in this case focuses on a matter of tourism to a large extent.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I believe that the focus of your research has since changed. Could you tell the Court when that happened and what is now the major focus of your research?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes, my interest and work on the sociology of tourism really extended from principally 1983 up until things began to go wrong in Yugoslavia in about 1989. After that, not only did tourism decline in its importance in that region but also other aspects of the political structure and process in Yugoslavia began to attract much greater attention and I began to switch my activities to that, publishing first of all a substantial review in a book edited by Professor Steven White of Glasgow University which was a review of reconstruction in all of the former socialist states of Europe - I wrote the chapter on Yugoslavia - and then moving into more specifically political concerns with two contributions to books published by the London publishing house Longmans which were studies of the formation of new political parties in Eastern Europe, and in both editions of that work I produced the chapters dealing with the former Yugoslav states.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you talked about publications which were commissioned by the publishing house Longmans. Can you talk about perhaps the commission from Longmans publishing house with respect to the year 1991.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Well, this was an interesting proposition, because, as I've already indicated to the Court, until that time the greater part of my research activity had been concerned with tourism. And the invitation to look at the emerging political parties and electoral processes in the former Yugoslavia was a relatively novel idea for me. So I made it a condition of my accepting the commission that I would be able to put together a package of funding that would enable me to do fieldwork in the area to support what I had to say. And with assistance, both from my own university as well as from the publisher and from some other sources as well, I put together enough money to enable me to make a systemic tour of all of the republics of the former Yugoslavia in which I was able to interview leading figures in the various political parties, to gather appropriate information, to look at public opinion polls and this kind of thing. So that that tour took me throughout the Federation and indeed was one of the occasions on which I was able to visit Dubrovnik. My stay in Croatia coincided with the referendum run by the Tudjman government on the question of Croatian independence and I was travelling in Croatia, including Dubrovnik, at the time of that referendum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What month would that have been, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I believe it was May 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a few more questions before we tender your expert report. Are you conversant with the language of Bosnian/Serbo-Croat, otherwise known as B/C/S in this institution?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: It wasn't known as that when I was there at the time, but yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this the first time that you have given evidence in the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: No, this is the second occasion. I was invited by the Office of the Prosecutor to serve in this same capacity in connection with the trial of Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the nature of your testimony in that case, as far as your expertise is concerned?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: On that occasion I was asked to provide a broad background overview of some aspects of society and politics, principally in Bosnia-Herzegovina but also because it was relevant to the case to some extent also dealing with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Maybe at this point we could formally tender your expert report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I request that it be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the expert report would be Exhibit P14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have a copy of your report in front of you, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Do the Bench have a copy of the report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. One member of the Bench, two members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: We're making progress.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Allcock, now that we've established your expertise in the matter of Yugoslavian affairs, I'd like to ask you when you first became acquainted with Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: My first visit to Dubrovnik, I believe, was in the spring of -- no, the summer of 1981. This was a private visit I made on the way to attend a function in Macedonia. My systematic acquaintance with Dubrovnik really began in 1983 when I started my research into the sociology of tourism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many times have you been to Dubrovnik in total?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I really couldn't tell you exactly how many times, but I can give you an indication in that from 1983 up until 1991, my research into the sociology of tourism regularly took me to Dubrovnik. I was certainly there at least on one occasion in each of those years, and some of those stays would be really quite protracted, of more than a month. And I believe on one occasion, at least one occasion, certainly one occasion, I was there for two months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you acquainted with the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with its monuments?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we may turn to the main body of your evidence. The first issue I'd like to refer you to is the section where you talk about the Old Town in general.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you perhaps start by clarifying the distinction between the municipality of Dubrovnik and the Old Town of Dubrovnik in particular.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes. The phrase the "Old Town" refers generally to the area lying within the fortified walls of the city. Building land is really rather scarce, however, along the Dalmatian coast, because high and rather steep hills, very bare hills, come very close to the sea for the greater part of that coastline. Consequently, when it was no longer possible to accommodate everybody within the Old Town itself, building expanded beyond that and has extended in a linear fashion along the coast. The first area in which this settlement expanded was to the north-west, the area known as Gruz, around the new port there. But generally speaking, since that time, since the 19th century, building has continued to expand along the coast in a rather diffuse fashion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you talk about the spatial area of the Old Town of Dubrovnik, and you state in your report that it was 13.38 hectares. Now, I would Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. like you to comment if you could, perhaps, on the density of the population that lived within that confined space.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes. It's difficult to be exact about population density in this respect because the census figures, the official published statistics for Croatia only give settlement figures by municipality. And as you'll see from my report, there were, of the 1991 census, more than 71.000 people living in that larger municipality. It would be necessary to go back to the original census documentation, which I have not been able to do, in order to determine exactly how many people lived within the city walls. This is quite a substantial number, however. I don't know exactly how many, but I would guess that it is possibly about 7 or 8.000 people live there. That is a guesstimate rather than anything else. It is fairly densely settled, however, within the city walls. This is not just a space occupied by monuments, it is a city in which people live.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you describe, perhaps, features of the type of the living accommodation within the walls of the Old Town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes, with the exception of the main thoroughfare which runs down the centre of the town, known as the stratum, the streets are really rather narrow on the whole and bordered on each side by old houses going back sometimes into the early medieval period, which usually extend to about four floors. Now, when they were originally constructed, many of these buildings were really rather grand. They tend to be known even today as palaces but in fact they're what in Britain would probably be known as rather stately townhouses. Because of the change in the social structure and economic structure of Dubrovnik, these are no longer occupied by single noble families, as they would be at the time of their construction. They've since been divided into flats, apartments, and I don't know whether any of these large old houses still are single-family occupied. I doubt very much that any of them are. So that, bearing in mind the multi-occupancy of these buildings, separated by really rather narrow streets, I think it's possible to assume that the density of the population within the Old Town is fairly high.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the last paragraph of the section entitled The Old Town of Dubrovnik, you talk about the boundaries of the municipality of Dubrovnik. Perhaps you could slightly elaborate on that matter; how they were formed, perhaps, throughout the ages

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes, the boundaries of the municipality, with some small changes, really go back into antiquity and, for the most part, follow the borders of the medieval Republic of Radusa, which was the name given to Dubrovnik in an earlier incarnation. This means that although Dubrovnik is part of the Republic of Croatia and in its north-westward extension continues into other municipalities of the republic, on the England side, the north-eastern side and eastern side, the border of the municipality itself forms the border of the Republic of Croatia with the neighbouring Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The municipality tapers to a very fine point just short of -- down near the Gulf of Kotor, the Bay of Kotor, at which point it touches on the Republic of Montenegro, and at that point also formerly constituted the inter-republican boundary within Yugoslavia; now, of course, that has become an international boundary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as your evidence progresses, we will talk about specific features of the Old Town of Dubrovnik, but before we get to that, I would like to have Exhibit P9 put in front of you. That is the map entitled "The Times Map of the Western Balkans."

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here we can perhaps see part of the boundaries of the municipality of Dubrovnik, at the lower part of the map.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would like to refer you to -- or perhaps ask you to comment on the town that we can see called Trebinje. This is a town which will have significance as this case progresses. I would like you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: First of all, I would inquire whether or not the Trial Chamber has identified the town of Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Due east of Dubrovnik, about three quarters of an inch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Allcock, what can you tell us about Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Well, Trebinje is located in Bosnia and Herzegovina and indeed in that part of Herzegovina usually called Eastern Herzegovina. It's in many respects rather different from Dubrovnik, and indeed the coastal area generally. The separation of that inland area from the coast by high hills has meant that not only topographically is it very different, but as a consequence of that, the type of agriculture, the type of economy, the way of life, has developed very differently. Also, Trebinje will have been part of the Ottoman Empire in the period before the departure of the Turks from the area in 1912, 1913. And indeed before then it was part of the Austrian domination of Bosnia. So that its history in many respects has been different from that of Dubrovnik. As you can probably see from the map, although it is part of a different republic, the natural lines of communication which connect Trebinje with the outside world, generally speaking, are poor, but a significant line of contact and communication is with the coast and with Dubrovnik. It -- a good deal of the economic life of Trebinje was connected with that of Dubrovnik, and in particular through the activity of tourism. As I'm sure the Court will be familiar, tourism is a highly seasonal activity which attracts very large amounts of labour for limited seasons of the year. And Dubrovnik had in this respect an enormous attractive potential which extended through a large part of its hinterland and a good deal of its seasonal labour was drawn in from Eastern Herzegovina and indeed from much more widely afield from that. And that road that you can see on the map there connecting Trebinje with Dubrovnik is really very significant for the economic social communication -- or has been in the past before they became part of two separate states, was very important as a means of communication between the two towns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Allcock. Now, perhaps succinctly, a few words on the ethnicity of the place Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: As I suggested, the two towns are very significantly different in their social structure and certainly that is true in the case of their ethnicity as well. Not being advised of this question before I came here, I haven't had a chance to look up exactly what the proportion of different ethnic groups is in Trebinje, but it is certainly a town with a substantial preponderance of ethnic Serbs. I believe also that there were a significant number of ethnic Muslims there before the war, but certainly it was the case that by far the largest proportion of its population were ethnic Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: This is not so of Dubrovnik, of course, and figures in that respect are given in my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I promised, we will now turn to some features of the Dubrovnik municipality and region. I would like to exhibit a photograph for you. If you could look at your video monitor, hopefully you will see this.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Not yet -- oh, I see, I have to press something. We have a photograph, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good. Now, you were talking about contours and hills overlooking Dubrovnik before. Perhaps you could use this diagram -- sorry, this picture, as a means of elaborating.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Right, yes. I have no idea what the numbers 28 and 909 mean, but ignoring those I think it's possible to see, looking at those contour lines, the way in which they're rather steeply clustered in a line running from the top left to bottom right of the picture, this indicates that on the seaward side, the bottom left-hand side, there's quite a steep slope, generally speaking -- and I've lost the picture now. There's quite a steep slope separates that coastal area from the inland area of -- right, I've got my picture back now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the red blob, just for the sake of clarification, is the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Represents the Old Town, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good. Now, perhaps with the aid of the map which is exhibited to your right we can see a few more features. I'm afraid this map is not in video presentation --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Am I allowed to leave my seat at this point to point to things?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could. Now, sir, could you point out where Mount Srdj is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there a microphone?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask the question. If you can just point and return to your seat.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Mount Srdj, you can see this area here is the Old City --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you would perhaps just pause a moment. We're trying to overcome the technical problem which will ensure that your evidence is recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is that working now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: We can move on, Your Honours, if this is time-consuming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: One on the other side, perhaps, might be easier to reach.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I stand on this side, perhaps this microphone -- are we audible now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Keep your voice clear, as seems not to be a problem for you, Mr. Allcock, and I hope the interpreters will manage to pick you up and the sound recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This here is the Old Town of Dubrovnik. This is the coastline of the Old Town. The steep ground, as I mentioned, runs immediately inland there and Mount Srdj is this highland area here, which is immediately to the north-east of the -- of the Old Town. And that area -- that there, the point immediately due north of the Old Town is the submit of the mountain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is on the summit of that mountain, do you know?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: There are old fortifications there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you could return to your seat, sir, I will show you a photograph on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Hopefully that photograph is being displayed on Your Honours' monitors as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Are we still functioning?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see a photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I do see a photograph, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mount Srdj, is it visible enough?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Mount Srdj is visible in the top right hand of the picture, yes, where the pointer is now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, perhaps you could elaborate on the historic significance of Mount Srdj, give us an example.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes, Mount Srdj represents a really rather fateful experience in the former history of the area, in that, as my report indicates, the city of Dubrovnik was the centre of an independent republic city state from early medieval times up until the beginning of the 19th century. During the Napoleonic wars, Napoleon extended his control over increasingly large parts of the Adriatic - and I don't think the details of that process concern us at the moment - but in the early part of 1806, Napoleon's Marshal Marmont, who had been threatening the town for a little while, succeeded in getting his canon on the top of Mount Srdj, at which point the citizens of Dubrovnik decided that cooperation was probably a better policy than resistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you look at my pointer, hopefully I'm pointing at a road.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: A road, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I believe that is the Adriatic highway. This is very important in the development of Dubrovnik, because prior to the 1960s the greater part of communication between Dubrovnik and the outside world had to take place by sea, certainly the great part of communication along the Adriatic coast, for various reasons, that was very difficult. Then in the early 1960s, Yugoslavia obtained substantial foreign credits which enabled it to build a road all the way down the Adriatic coast. This had an immediate and dramatic impact upon the development of tourism in the entire area. And I'm not sure exactly when the road reached Dubrovnik, but Dubrovnik certainly benefited as part of that general opening up by means of the Adriatic highway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please, if you would, look at the next photograph. Here we see, where my arrow is pointing, can you tell the Court?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes, that is the old port of Dubrovnik, the old medieval port, which was protected, as the Court can see from the photograph, by the city walls and the boom across its mouth. That port, unfortunately, ceased to serve the needs of the town with the advent of steam navigation during the 19th century. And the greater part of commercial maritime activity moved during the 19th century north-westwards along the coast over the hill to Gruz which then opened up as a new port which was big enough and deep enough to take modern steamships. And since the later part, certainly since the last quarter of the 19th century, the old port there, which you see in the picture, has only served as an anchorage for visiting pleasure boats and tripping ships of one kind or another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please, sir, follow my arrow.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The arrow is tracing a path --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes, that is the thoroughfare to which I've already referred, the main axial thoroughfare of the Old Town of Dubrovnik, known as the stradun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: This is a picture of the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you elaborate on something perhaps conspicuous about this photograph? It was photographed on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Two things strike me about the photograph: One is that it illustrates very well the type of housing which I mentioned in the earlier part of my remarks, the multi-storey accommodation, fairly closely spaced, suggesting the density of population in the town; but the first thing which strikes one when one sees this picture is that there are no human beings in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the normal situation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Well, I have never seen the stradun looking like that. It is normally busy from early in the morning until very late at night. Although there is a car shown there, it's largely a pedestrian thoroughfare so that, for the most part, it's a very busy scene of pedestrians walking up and down. In the evening, incidentally, it becomes a particularly significant social centre where people come to walk and meet and use the cafes which are found in the ground floor of those buildings along the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, moving to -- back to the previous photograph and to the next section of your expert report, which is entitled "The Architectural Heritage of Dubrovnik," you mentioned the fortifications of Dubrovnik. Here we see the fortifications. Perhaps you could elaborate on the fortifications.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I've lost the single again, but I can certainly elaborate on what I saw in it, yes, and on the nature of the fortifications. The fortifications were built over quite a long period of time, from the early medieval period. I think they were probably completed in the 17th century, if my memory serves me correctly. They've been particularly important in the life of the town, because being a very small independent city state, Dubrovnik had virtually no armed forces. And so, for its defensive capability it relied almost exclusively upon two things, one is the enormous strength of its fortifications, and the other thing, of course, was the skill of its diplomats who tried to head off trouble in the first place. But I gather that those walls are a remarkable example of late medieval and early modern fortification. The thickness of them is really quite astonishing in places. I did have some correspondence with the city planning authorities about this in the process of preparing my report, and although my report indicates that the area inside the city walls is 13.38 hectares, the total area occupied, including the walls, is 15 hectares. So you can see that a fairly substantial area is covered by those walls, which indicates their enormous strength in places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this photograph was taken after 1991.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after what appears to be the restoration of the Old Town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see the roof tiles of the roofs. Could you perhaps comment on the nature of the roof tiles prior to 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes. There is a very visible difference between what one would have seen before 1991 and what is displayed in this picture. It is possible to see, if you look closely, a few areas of undamaged tiling. These appear, if you look closely, as a lighter, browner shade. Yes, where the arrow is pointing now, the roof of the Franciscan monastery there is still showing that lighter colour. The sight of the roofs of Dubrovnik was one of the most attractive features of the town before the war. As I'm sure the Court will be able to imagine, with several centuries of aging, the roofs had acquired a kind of irregularity through the contraction and twisting of timbers. And with tiles being replaced over a long period of time, and with those tiles not being the result of modern factory production but of a rather haphazard craft production, you had an extremely interesting surface represented by those tiles; variegated colouring, subtle shades of difference, subtle differences in form because of the way in which the roofs had settled and shrunk over time. That has now been replaced by the regular forms of the replacement roofs in many places where the structures had to be replaced and certainly even where it's only been necessary to replace the tiling, the uniform colouring of modern factory-produced tiles. At one time before the war, certainly it was the case that one of the preferred activities of tourists in the region, to the town, was to walk around the walls simply in order to observe and enjoy the view of the old roofs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we can move on now to a totally different part of your report, and I would like to take you to the part of your report which deals with tourism and the effect of the conflict in Dubrovnik on tourism. What was the importance of tourism for Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Tourism was of extreme importance to Dubrovnik. The entire Adriatic coast was extremely poor between the -- I suppose the -- particularly the end of the 18th century and the early part of the 20th century. A very substantial out-migration took place from those areas because of the inability of the population to feed themselves. Large numbers of the contemporary inhabitants of Australia, parts of South America and North America hail from Dalmatia. Indeed among anthropologists looking at the region previously, Dalmatia was known as a passive region. In other words, it was not able to actively support itself, it relied entirely upon the import of foodstuffs. Although tourism began to take root in the later part, last quarter of the 19th century, and indeed enjoyed some success during the inter-war years, the years between World Wars I and II, it was really only with the arrival of the road, which we've already examined, in the 1960s that mass tourism became impossible down the Adriatic coast. And at that point the economic fortunes of Dubrovnik were reversed and the Adriatic coast as a whole, including Dubrovnik, instead of being among the poorest and most destitute parts of Yugoslavia became one of the most prosperous areas of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the effect of the Balkan conflict on that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: The effect of the Balkan conflict was to bring that process crashing to a standstill. I think that a very good illustration of this is given in the table which I provide --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's on page 17 --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: That's correct. Figure 1 on page 17, which provides graphically there accounts of the number of nights spent by tourists -- these are figures for Croatia as a whole -- the number of nights spent by tourists from Croatia and the number of nights spent by foreign tourists. We can Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. see that as early as 1989, when the political condition of Yugoslavia became steadily more unstable, there was an accelerating process of the decline of tourism, especially the significance of foreign tourism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And perhaps that would explain, if I can refer you to page 12 of your expert report, the first sentence, you talk about the decline of visitors in Dubrovnik to 33,489 in 1990, which is in fact before the time of the conflict relevant to this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. Tourism is an extremely sensitive aspect of business from the point of view of risk. At the first sign of risk, tourists become very reluctant to visit an area, and although open armed conflict had not begun in 1989 and 1990, already tourists were sensing the political instability and risk of Yugoslavia and were refraining from taking their holidays there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Well, I think that, to a large extent, clarifies your report. Before I conclude the review of your report I would just perhaps like to refer you to the appendices attached to your report and ask you if there's anything you wish to clarify. We've already dealt with the graph on page 17, perhaps the graph on page 18.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes, the graph on page 18 is really intended to convey something of the same information. The light grey figures in -- the horizontal bars indicate the volume of tourists coming from particular countries to Croatia in different years: The top bar, 1989; the white bar in the middle, 1993; and the bottom bar 1994. And if you compare in particular the first and second of those bars, figures for 1989 and figures for 1993, roughly pre and post the armed conflict which is the subject of this particular court case, that gives a very dramatic visual indication of the decline of tourists from different foreign countries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, at this point I would like to tender the photographs that we displayed on the video monitor to the Court. There are four in total.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would conclude your examination-in-chief, which shouldn't take more than ten minutes, hopefully, by asking you to comment on some of the Defence submissions that have been made in respect of your expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: So if those photographs could be submitted at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the photograph depicting the features of Dubrovnik would be Exhibit P15. The photograph of Mount Srdj would be P16. The photograph of the old port of Dubrovnik would be P17. And the photograph of the thoroughfare of Dubrovnik P18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I would like to address you briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not wish to give any suggestions on how the cross-examination should be conducted; however, I think that it would be appropriate to say that -- what I'm trying to say should probably come out in cross-examination. And that is because our submission under Rule 74 bis was of a summary nature. It did not contain facts or arguments that perhaps would have been appropriate. Therefore, to the extent that the Defence does have some objections to the opinion of this witness I think would have been better to point that out in the cross-examination rather than in this way because our submission, as I have said, was of an informative nature and did not go to the substance of the matter. However, I will leave it to your discretion to make a decision concerning this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm not entirely clear the point you make. I'm sorry, Mr. Petrovic. I gather you don't object to the tendering of the report, but you wanted to be received subject to the submission -- to the cross-examination that you will put and perhaps to some other submissions. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I wasn't clear enough; and if I wasn't, I apologise to you for that. Therefore, the issue of admissibility of this report, I believe this issue to have been already resolved by your ruling concerning this report. Therefore, there is no sense in our objecting or not objecting to it now. What I was trying to say is that some objections that we have concerning this should probably come out during our cross-examination rather than be interpreted now through the questions put by my learned colleague. That is the essence of what I'm trying to say, however it is naturally up to you decide. And I apologise if I wasn't clear initially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm grateful for your comments, Mr. Petrovic. May I firstly indicate as a matter of general practice to both Prosecution and Defence that when an exhibit is tendered to the Court, if I do not detect that there is objection by the opposing party, I will simply admit the document. I did not notice that you proposed to object, and so I received the report as I did. In future, if there is an objection to an exhibit, I'd be grateful if it -- you make that known, and this is for both parties, at the time it is tendered and we can deal with the objection. Your particular concern is that Mr. Kaufman now proposes to put questions that anticipate to some way, from what he said, what you propose to be putting in cross-examination. That's the concern. Let me explore that with Mr. Kaufman a little, if you would. Yes, Mr. Kaufman, perhaps you could elaborate just a little what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I understood Mr. Petrovic's first submission, on which there was in fact a ruling on the 12th of December, 2003, to refer purely to the procedural aspect of whether or not Dr. Allcock had expertise sufficient in order to enable him to testify before this Tribunal. The Court decided on that matter. However, within the framework of the Defence objections to that expert opinion, certain substantive matters were raised. And as far as I am aware, it's the practice of this Tribunal -- and certainly the practice in the jurisdiction from where I come, that it is perfectly permissible to anticipate Defence cross-examination by way of examination-in-chief insofar as those matters to which Defence take objection are critical to the issues before the Court. Otherwise, I may have no way of getting the Prosecution case across by way of evidence which may be led from this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything further you would like to put, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My reaction to your concern, Mr. Petrovic, is to suggest that it is already clear to both Prosecution and Defence and to the Trial Chamber that certain aspects of the report of the witness are to be challenged or questioned by you. And in my experience of these matters, it would be perfectly proper for Mr. Kaufman to be asking the witness to put his observations about those points of concern into evidence at this point of the Prosecution case. That in the long-term, I would suggest, is likely to have the advantage that you will then know exactly what it is that Mr. Allcock wants to say about those matters, and you can then shape your cross-examination with that knowledge. So in a sense, it is not only enabling the Prosecution to put what it wants, but it gives you some clear knowledge of how to shape your own cross-examination. So I would propose at this stage to allow Mr. Kaufman to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I withdraw my previous submissions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And I thank my learned friend for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Allcock, I would like to refer you to some submissions which were made within the Defence pre-trial brief which touch on the nature of your evidence. Perhaps if you could look at your monitor, I am displaying the relevant page of the Defence pre-trial brief. If you could perhaps read paragraph 22 --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I don't think I have got it yet. Shall I press a button or something? That's it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look at paragraph 22, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read that or would you like me to --
