utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I can read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last sentence in particular.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Well, this is a very commonly expressed opinion, but I think the consensus among social scientists these days would tend to challenge that. My interpretation of that sentence is that -- well, it doesn't need much interpretation. "... the unsettled national issue was the key reason for the disintegration of the second Yugoslav state." Two things emerge from that statement. First of all, the key status of what is called here "the national issue," and secondly the use of "the," the definite article. It suggests that this above all other things was the reason why the former Yugoslavia fell apart. I believe that the longer scholars go on looking at this issue, the more the national issue comes to be seen not so much as the primary cause for the disintegration of Yugoslavia in this fashion but as a consequence of processes of an economic and political nature and that the causal inference which is conveyed by this sentence needs to be reversed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I can elaborate on that if it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this moment in time it's not necessary, sir. If you could look at paragraph 23. I can enlarge that if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I can read it. I have read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps the Bench would like that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: I have it, right. It's interesting from a rhetorical point of view. The word "disguised" is heavily emotive, is it not? To me, this sentence suggests -- the phrase "the disguised Croatian separatism" suggests two things: First of all, it suggests that there is a single Croatian view which is being conveyed here, "the disguised Croatian separatism"; but also it suggests that somehow or another there is something going on here to conceal from general knowledge what are the real aims of Croatian politicians. Now, there may well have been Croatian politicians to whom the implication of this sentence applies. I believe that is the case. But from my familiarity with Croatian politics, it's by no means the case that Croatian views about -- we're talking here about the pre-1991 period, the period when Croatia was anticipating some kind of change of its status in relation to the Yugoslav state. It certainly is not my recollection that there was a uniform view among Croatian politicians that the only future for Croatia was separation from the Yugoslav state. It certainly was the case that the predominant opinion, I believe not only among Croatian politician but probably the public as well, was that some kind of redefinition was appropriate of the relationship between the various republics which made up the Federation and that greater autonomy for a Croatian republic was certainly desirable. But I don't believe that the implication is correct, conveyed by that sentence that somehow or another there was a single Croatian view about the future of Yugoslavia. That separatism was desirable and that there was some kind of, well maybe conspiracy is to put it too strongly, but there was some kind of attempt to conceal the real intentions of Croatia in relation to the future of the republic. I don't believe that those assumptions are correct. So that I would want to challenge that statement fairly strongly. Again, I would be happy to elaborate on that opinion, should it be necessary, but in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. The last item in the Defence pre-trial brief which I would like to draw your attention to is to found at paragraphs 43 and 44. Unfortunately, I have a slight technical problem here so I can't display that page in front of you but I will let you know what it contains. This is about the exploitation of propaganda, the alleged, if I may put it, exploitation of propaganda by the Croatians. Can you perhaps comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: What is the specific phrase on which I am required to comment?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do actually have a copy here of the Defence pre-trial brief, so I shall read it out for you. I will ask the usher to place a copy of that in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you remind me of the number of the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it's paragraphs 43 and 44. If I may read them out for you. "Croatia's top officials in Zagreb and military commanders located in Dubrovnik knew very well that the events around Dubrovnik could be availed of exceptionally beneficially as a means in the propaganda war against JNA, SFRY, and in the battle for gaining independence. Croatian side conscientiously transformed Dubrovnik into a military target." Paragraph 44 in the language of the Defence counsel: "Moreover, by operating from the immediate proximity of the Old Town, very often from the very centre of the Old Town as well, Croatian side was provoking the fire of the opposite party which it then skillfully used for propaganda purposes well aware of the degree of sensitivity of the international community when endangering of valuable monuments of history and culture is concerned." Could you comment on that, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ALLCOCK
utterances.text: Well, my first comment is that in many respects these two sentences are referring to events which neither figure in my report nor upon which I have any direct means of commenting. As I've already indicated, my last presence in Dubrovnik before the outbreak of hostility was May 1991, and so I have no means of commenting upon the -- whether or not Dubrovnik was transformed into a military target. I have no direct observation of those things. But as a sociologist who has taught courses on mass communication before, once again the rhetorical structure of these paragraphs does leap to my attention. And it is certainly the case, it is certainly the case, that the military activities surrounding Dubrovnik in the winter of 1991 became extremely important factors in the way in which international public opinion perceived the events in the former Yugoslavia. I would say that probably during the course of the armed conflict, three events have probably equalled each other in the way in which they have attracted public -- and formed public opinion outside Yugoslavia with respect to the events in that country. The first of these would be the siege and eventual capture of Vukovar. The second would be the siege of Dubrovnik, or military activity surrounding Dubrovnik. And the third would be the long-running siege of Sarajevo. Now, all of those events certainly were commented upon very freely, very fully in the press outside of Yugoslavia and had a powerful role in forming public opinion about the nature of the conflict there. So much I would certainly agree with. These two paragraphs contain an additional implication, however, which I think it's appropriate to draw to the attention of the Court that go beyond what I've said, and that is contained in the last sentence, certainly, of paragraph 43: "The Croatian side conscientiously transformed Dubrovnik into a military target." This suggests that the propaganda value of a military attack on the city was anticipated by the Croatian authorities, and that any disposition of Croatian military forces in the area of Dubrovnik took place with the intention of bringing about events that could be exploited for propaganda purposes. Now, as I say, I have no -- I had no direct access to the Croatian leadership of this time, so I'm not able to comment on the truth or falsity of that claim. I merely comment on it in my capacity, as I say, as a sociologist accustomed to analysing mass communication. But it certainly remains to be demonstrated that that was the case. And nothing in my report could be said to either contribute to that view or to challenge it, it's simply outside the competence of my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I thank you very much for your help and for clarifying Dubrovnik in its cultural, historic and economic context. That concludes the examination-in-chief. I'm afraid you will have to come back next year to be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kaufman. And you will have gathered from that, Mr. Allcock, that the circumstances are such that on the 12th of January we will continue, and the cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you mind if I consult my diary for a moment, because your mention of the 12th of diary rings a bell. Is it possible to assure me that I will be able to be in Oxford on the 13th of January? I am very reluctant indeed to inconvenience this Tribunal, and if it is important, then I can change my arrangement in Oxford, but I simply point out that I have a commitment in Oxford on the 13th of January. If you would really like me to make that effort, I will do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I can be of assistance to Mr. Allcock. We shall do everything in our power to complete it on the 12th, so I hope that you will be able to go home either on the 12th in the evening or on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will be available on the 12th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am not wanting to put a -- what I would call a spanner in the works about this, but unfortunately, on the 12th it will not be possible for us to resume sitting before 3.00, that is three quarters of an hour later than usual. Now, will that still leave you time enough, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we press all systems green or go, Mr. Allcock, for the 12th of January, and your evidence should conclude that day, and hopefully you will be able to meet your commitment the next day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, if you wouldn't mind just sitting there for a moment while I turn to a few other matters. Just a couple of procedural matters first, Mr. Weiner. First, Mr. Weiner, the issue of the witnesses and the order that they'll be called, are you in a position to confirm the informal indication you gave to the staff I think earlier this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. We believe it's going to be now Allcock and then hopefully Davies, Samardzic and Alajbeg with the possibility of the witness Peko following Allcock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will be aware, of course, of the need -- for the purpose of ensuring the smooth running of these matters and the availability of the necessary documents, exhibits, et cetera, for there to be an ongoing clear indication of the order of witnesses. So if you could just confirm with the staff when we rise exactly what that order will be in the first week, I would be grateful. Now, there was the issue of the proofing charts. Is that one that has now been dealt with?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It just has to be printed out, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So that will be in the hands of the Tribunal this afternoon, will it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes; that takes one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good. We had earlier indicated our ambition to deliver our reasons on the Rule 92 bis application of the Prosecution by today. For two particular reasons we are not in a position to do. Two matters which we find bear directly on the 92 bis application are yet to be the subject of written submissions. They are, of course, in respect of the witness Nikola Jovic and, more significantly, there is the Defence objection to the admission of evidence relating to events other than the 6th of December, 1991, and the determination of the Prosecution application in respect of a significant number of the witnesses involve consideration of that issue. So we are not in a position to oblige you with that ruling at this point, I'm sorry, Mr. Weiner, but could I suggest that for the purposes of planning the early stages of the New Year, that you ought to proceed on the basis that if the evidence of a witness which is -- who is the subject of the Rule 92 bis application is seen to be required in the early stages, then that witness should attend in person. I have -- turning now to a further matter, I've already indicated that, unfortunately, it will not be possible to commence sitting before 3.00 on Monday the 12th. The one remaining matter is the motion of the Defence for a medical examination of the accused pursuant to Rule 74 bis. There has been prepared, and it is now published, a short decision of this Trial Chamber. For the reasons there indicated, we have not been persuaded that we have reason to order a full and further medical examination of the accused, so the motion does not succeed. But we have and do request the Registrar of the Tribunal to ensure that during the adjournment, during the three-week break, the accused is kept under observation by a doctor of medicine and that should there be any deterioration in his general physical or medical condition, that that be reported to the Tribunal. And of course, we do note in the decision that our action in no way precludes the Defence themselves commissioning a report on the health and condition of the accused if that is thought to be necessary at this point. We will now adjourn for the break. We would wish everybody an enjoyable break and the compliments of the season.
